item.title: Why Vanderbilt and the Whitney Museum Are Partners
item.description:
Good morning. It’s Monday. Today we’ll find out about what a partnership with the Whitney Museum of American Art will mean for undergraduates at Vanderbilt University’s new Manhattan outpost.

I had a question for Scott Rothkopf, who figures in Vanderbilt University’s we’ll-take-Manhattan strategy. The question was: When was the last time he taught a class?

“You mean like a professor and do a whole seminar?” he said. “I have never taught a full semester. I have spent a lot of time talking with students and interns and doing crits with art students, where you go to their studio and review their work together.”

But Rothkopf, the director of the Whitney Museum of American Art, said he expected to do some teaching, thanks to Vanderbilt. “I think I will,” he said.

Vanderbilt and the Whitney have arranged a partnership that will involve students with the museum. The Whitney and Vanderbilt are sort-of neighbors, now that Vanderbilt has leased the General Theological Seminary’s campus in Chelsea (through a $44 million, 99-year deal that was announced last fall), and the first cohort of 85 undergraduates have taken up residence on the neo-Gothic quadrangle. For Vanderbilt, “it’s almost like you take a piece of Vanderbilt’s natural campus” — in Nashville, not quite 900 miles from Chelsea — “and teleport it to New York,” said Daniel Diermeier, Vanderbilt’s chancellor.

Vanderbilt has an ambitious plan for satellite campuses in several U.S. cities at a time when many of its peer institutions are retrenching. “The premise is, we believe the era of the ivory tower university is over,” Diermeier said. “It’s about creating opportunities for students and our faculty that would be difficult if we were confined to Nashville.”

He said that Vanderbilt’s home base was well suited to providing undergraduate instruction, training health care practitioners with its medical school and offering specialization in the entertainment industry with its proximity to the Grand Ole Opry and the rest of Nashville’s music scene. A presence in New York puts Vanderbilt students in a financial center. Vanderbilt arranged for Diermeier to ring the opening bell at the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square the morning before classes began last month.

Diermeier also said that New York had become increasingly important for Vanderbilt as the university remade itself as a more selective school: Its incoming class has more students from the New York area than anywhere else, he said.

One reason, according to Diermeier, is Vanderbilt’s appeal to Jewish students since the Oct. 7 Hamas attack on Israel almost three years ago. “We got through that much more successfully than our peer schools,” he said. “This ostracizing, what happened at other universities where students were ostracized or excluded because of their beliefs, that just didn’t happen at Vanderbilt.”

And then there is the Whitney. Diermeier called the partnership with the museum “one of the clearest examples of what we can’t do in Nashville.”

“We don’t have a Whitney in Nashville,” he said.

Vanderbilt’s arrival dovetails with the Whitney’s push to reach younger audiences. Rothkopf, who called the Vanderbilt cohort “a natural fit,” noted that the Whitney already offered free admission every Friday and one Sunday a month for everyone 25 and under.

But the partnership, which the Whitney sees as a reciprocal model for how a museum can partner with a university and the surrounding community, will go further. Much further, Rothkopf said.

“Quite a few museums that partner with major universities tend to focus on graduate students in art history,” Rothkopf said. The Vanderbilt group probably includes students whose interest in art could carry them through to graduate school, but many are likely to go in other directions.

Under the partnership, Vanderbilt students will serve as interns “not just in our curatorial department but in marketing and education,” Rothkopf said. “Those are the kinds of internships that could lead to careers in other nonprofits or different jobs beyond the art world. If you’re a marketing intern at the Whitney, there are lots of possible things you’ll learn that would be interesting outside the confines of a museum.”

He said that the museum was in discussions for more than a year. Soon after the talks began, “I said, ‘Why don’t we dream bigger’” than just arranging internships, he said. “We’re a cultural anchor in this neighborhood you are now calling your home. It also has world-class art galleries just steps from where you are, and the Shed. Could we be a portal for you to this whole world?”

Weather

A sunny day is ahead with temperatures near 76. Tonight, expect mostly clear skies and a low around 58.

ALTERNATE-SIDE PARKING

In effect until Sept. 21 (Yom Kippur).

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Absolutely nothing has happened.” — Jason Froimowitz, the transportation committee chairman of Manhattan Community Board 6, on the lack of progress on a plan to create a “busway” on a one-mile stretch of 34th Street. It’s been three months since Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the long-delayed project was moving forward.

A big expansion for small farms: Farm to People, a Brooklyn-based online grocer working with over 200 farms in and around New York City, announced its first outside investment of $5 million, which it says it will use to open a 40,000-square-foot facility in the Bronx in 2027.

Judge Judy steps down: Judith Sheindlin, a former supervising judge of Manhattan Family Court whose “Judge Judy” show once dominated daytime television, is ending her television career. The last episode of “Judy Justice,” the Amazon Prime spinoff of the program that made her a household name, will be released on Oct. 22.

A permanent home: The Martha Graham Dance Company, the oldest dance troupe in the country, is taking over 21,000 square feet of the Paramount Building, a Times Square landmark. The new location will accommodate the company’s 17 dancers; roughly 500 students; staff members; and storage for costumes, props and archival materials.

From sailors’ quarters to prison to housing: A building at West 20th Street and 11th Avenue was once a landing spot for merchant sailors and then a prison. Now, it’s being overhauled as part of a $167 million affordable housing project.

Your neighborhood Chinese dumpling spot: New York City’s love for Chinese dumplings is no less ardent today than it was in the 1980s, when dumpling shops became fixtures in Manhattan. Here are some local spots.

METROPOLITAN diary

Dear Diary:

I have been reading about Rao’s, at the corner of Pleasant Avenue and East 114th Street, for years. It is notoriously hard to get a table there, but it was on my bucket list. One day, I decided to try.

Arriving at the bright-red storefront at the bottom of a nondescript apartment building, I encountered what appeared to be a half-dozen regulars in suits mingling at the bar.

I took a seat on one of the stools.

“What do you want?” the bartender asked gruffly.

“Manhattan, please,” I replied, a slight trepidation in my voice.

He made the drink and put it in front of me.

“Can I eat dinner at the bar?” I asked.

“No,” he barked. “And the wait list is 10 years.”

The drink was beyond stiff, all the better to savor while stretching out the evening.

The small number of tables were soon packed with beefy types and laden with hefty dishes of pasta. Raucous laughter filled the room.

Two women in their early 20s sat next to me at the bar, and we began to talk. They lived in the neighborhood. We chatted for the better part of an hour about affordable housing, social causes and Spanish Harlem.

Suddenly, the women got up and wished me a good night. I turned and saw an older man gesturing them toward his table.

I finished my drink, paid the check and left. Ravenously hungry, I devoured a sack of White Castle sliders while walking the mile home.

— Kayvan Gabbay

Illustrated by Agnes Lee. Tell us your New York story here and read more Metropolitan Diary here.

Glad we could get together here. See you tomorrow. — J.B.

Davaughnia Wilson and Ed Shanahan contributed to New York Today. You can reach the team at nytoday@nytimes.com.

item.title: Meet a College Student Who Picks Up the Dead
item.description:
The shofar — that curved ram’s horn — is sounding today in synagogues. It’s the second day of Rosh Hashana, the beginning of the year 5787. The ba’alei tekiah, or masters of the blast, will blow 100 sounds in a special pattern throughout morning services.

The horn is intended to be a sort of communal alarm clock. “Awake, you sleepers, from your sleep; rouse yourselves, you slumberers, from your slumber,” Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher, instructed. The goal, at the start of this period, known as the Days of Awe, is to awaken to the fact that life is finite.

I want to introduce you to someone who is good at doing that, all the time.

Frankie Halvey spends his days on the leafy, redbrick campus of Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. He goes to classes for his public health major. He acts onstage for his theater minor. But at night, he leaves his phone on loud — ready to get a call, at any hour, that he needs to go pick up a dead body.

Frankie, at 20, is unusually familiar with death. The son of funeral directors in upstate New York, he worked through the Covid pandemic, when staff members were scarce and calls were not. He grew to appreciate the depth and meaning of the job, the way it let him extend care to people raw with grief. So he sought out similar shifts at college.

As a “transfer team member” at a funeral home, Frankie retrieves the bodies of the recently deceased from homes, hospitals and hospices. As many as four times a night, the phone rings and he pulls himself out of bed, climbs into a van and drives through rolling Amish farmland. He listens to music until he gets close to his destination.

“In the last five minutes of every drive I’ve ever done, I always take a little moment of silence,” he told me, “just to acknowledge the situation that I’m going to be walking into.”

Then he knocks on the door.

Standing there with a stretcher, Frankie will say hello, I’m so sorry for your loss, may I come in, where is your loved one. He tries to intuit what is needed. Sometimes that is silence. Other times people want to talk, and talk, and talk. They tell him what happened, how long it’s been like this, that they knew the end was coming, that they can’t believe it. Then they tell him stories about their mother’s favorite vacation, or what their father studied in school, or how they are sure their grandma really is with her husband now. Frankie listens, and when the talk tapers, he moves the deceased onto the stretcher. Then, if the body was in a bed, he spends time making it. He tucks the sheets and fluffs the pillows, smooths the duvet and folds the quilt. It’s what he can do, he said, to give the family dignity.

“I actually got that from my parents,” he said.

Once in a while, a bewildered spouse will stop him at the door. “They just ask me to sit in their home with them just so they don’t feel so alone,” he said. “After I leave, that person is probably going to be entirely alone for the rest of the night.”

I was taken by Frankie’s story, and it made me think of a book about the Jewish High Holy Days called “This Is Real and You Are Completely Unprepared.” The author, Rabbi Alan Lew, writes about those moments of intimate catastrophe that interrupt our hard-wired delusion — that other people will die, but not us. Rabbi Lew argues that the Days of Awe, which stretch between Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur, are a way to prepare for those moments.

“It’s a dress rehearsal for our death,” he writes of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, when God is said to finalize decisions about who will live and who will die in the coming year. “That’s why we wear a kittel, a shroud-like garment, on this day; why we refrain from life-affirming activities such as eating, drinking and procreating. We are rehearsing the day of our death.”

Frankie was raised Catholic and is now a member of an Episcopal church. But his job is also something of a dress rehearsal for the inevitable. He called it a spiritual reminder, one that helps him “try to live a meaningful life where I help others.”

That doesn’t mean it isn’t difficult. “There has never been a time where I’ve really felt great leaving a house call,” he told me. “People can be crying. People can be laughing. You really have no idea what you’re walking into.”

Still, he keeps taking shifts. As we talked about his long nights, I teared up at work thinking of a college student so selfless. It was my own small moment of awe, an example of the Jewish concept of chesed shel emet. That’s Hebrew for true kindness.

I met Frankie because he sent a submission to our new newsletter Extra Credit. If you’re in college, sign up! And if you know students who are in college, send them this link.

Do you wish someone a happy Jewish New Year by saying “l’shana tova” or “shana tova”? The Forward takes on the debate.

Speaking of, I loved this Tiny Love Story:

My baby is sandwiched between her grandpas: a Brooklyn-born Jew and a Vietnamese immigrant, each planting an exuberant kiss on her chubby cheeks. “What should I say for Jewish New Year?” my father asked shortly after I married. I was impressed he knew that there was one. We practiced “L’Shana tova.” When Lunar New Year arrived, my father-in-law called with a similar question. We practiced “Chuc mung nam moi.” Over the years, they exchanged loudly articulated, slightly unintelligible, but always well-intended greetings. As my baby and her younger siblings grew, so did the grandpas’ affection for their shared family. — Oanh Ngo Usadi

The British government announced that it would stop importing Israeli products manufactured or grown in the occupied West Bank. The foreign secretary went so far as to accuse some settlers of engaging in the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians.

The allies: Eleven countries — Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden — joined Britain in sanctioning the settlements.

The response: Israel, which has national elections at the end of October, ordered the closure of the British Consulate in Jerusalem. It also evicted British officials from a center coordinating support for Gaza and barred from the country a dozen British lawmakers and others it deemed anti-Israeli and antisemitic.

The impact: Exports from settlements are a fraction of the annual trade, worth $8 billion, between Britain and Israel. But income from goods like dates, wine and plastics is important to the finances of individual settlements.

The issue is dividing Jews in Britain during the holidays. Read more here.

This video of a young girl praying to her father after he died on Sept. 11, 2001.

James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, spoke with Jimmy Kimmel about progressive Christianity. (Watch the interview here.) Kimmel decided not to air the interview because of threats from the Federal Communications Commission about giving one candidate free airtime, so Kimmel’s producers put it on YouTube instead.

The brand Susan Alexandra, which makes accessories and Judaica, hosted its Best in Show dog show with designer Rachel Antonoff.

Jordan Schiffer, an artist who fuses graphic design and religious aesthetics.

“Unreconciled,” a play about clergy sexual abuse, explores what a community knows — and how suffering ripples beyond the victim. (The Revealer)

Reading: “The Renewal of Islam,” by Fitzroy Morrissey.

Also reading: I really liked this essay on control from Anne Snyder in Comment.

Marking: Rosh Hashana with a semi-observant friend. We’re bringing apples and honey on a hike in Wales.

Watching: “Super Nature,” a love letter to Earth shot on old film.

Thinking about: “Boomers,” a poem by George Bilgere. It’s about our serial inability to appreciate the good moments while we’re in them. I really recommend you read it.

Following: The School for Moral Ambition, a program focused on helping college students pursue pro-social work.

I love — I love — Poems on the Underground. It’s a public art project that displays verse where ads would normally go on London Tube. My favorite from this summer is “When I Was a Fish,” a poem by Krystyna Lenkowska that references reincarnation. Here’s a line, translated from Polish.

When I was a fishor a birdI didn’t need reputation

What would you do if your reputation didn’t matter? I’d still be writing this newsletter. See you next week!
